title: THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO STAY DISTANT
paragraphs: THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO STAY DISTANT
Why four words in John’s Gospel destroy our picture of a distant God—and reveal the staggering truth that Jesus Christ entered our wounded world to bring sinners from scandal to grace.
There are moments when God feels impossibly far away.
You pray, but the ceiling seems silent.
You open your Bible, but your mind keeps wandering back to the thing you regret.
You sit in church surrounded by people singing about victory while quietly wondering whether anyone would still look at you the same way if they knew everything.
The addiction you promised God you would stop.
The marriage nobody knows is barely surviving.
The resentment you disguise as discernment.
The prayer you have almost stopped praying because disappointment hurts less when you expect nothing.
And somewhere inside all of that, a terrifying question begins forming:
Does God really understand what it is like to be human?
John answers that question with one of the most breathtaking sentences ever written.
Not with advice about becoming a better person.
The Greek text of John 1:14 begins:
Those words are so familiar that Christians can read them without feeling their weight anymore.
But John did not write something safe.
The λόγος — Logos — the Word whom John has already identified at the beginning of his Gospel as existing “in the beginning,” as being “with God,” and as being God, became flesh.
Not merely visited humanity wearing a convincing disguise.
Not merely sent another prophet to tell suffering people how to find Him.

The Greek word John chooses is σάρξ — sarx — “flesh.” And the verb ἐγένετο — egeneto — means “became.” The language presents a real historical incarnation: the eternal Word truly entered human existence. Christian confession therefore does not mean that the Son stopped being divine and changed into something non-divine. It means that the One who eternally was the Word truly assumed humanity. John presents Jesus as genuinely divine and genuinely human.
Think about what John could have written.
He could have chosen language that kept everything polished and distant.
A heart that could experience anguish.
The One through whom John says everything came into existence stepped into the world that existed through Him.
The invisible God made Himself known in the Son.
And suddenly Christianity becomes something far more astonishing than humanity climbing upward toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to us.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to understand tonight.
You have spent years trying to climb.
Trying to repair yourself before approaching God.
You have thought, Once I defeat this sin, then I can really come back.
Once I stop looking at those things.
Once I become the Christian everyone thinks I already am.
But the Gospel begins by destroying the ladder.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter. The incarnation ultimately moves toward the cross precisely because sin matters terribly.
The Child of Bethlehem came to become the crucified Savior.
John will eventually bring us from:
The flesh He assumed could be wounded.
The hands that touched lepers could be nailed.
The feet that walked toward sinners could be pierced.
The head that knew every human thought could wear thorns.
The body through which divine compassion embraced the unwanted could hang upon a Roman cross.
Christianity does not proclaim a God watching human suffering through the safety of heaven.

And Hebrews makes the implications breathtaking: because Christ truly shared our humanity and was tempted yet without sin, believers do not approach a High Priest incapable of sympathizing with human weakness. We are invited to draw near to the throne of grace for mercy and help.
You are not explaining human pain to someone unfamiliar with humanity.
Jesus knew what it was to have people abandon Him.
Yet Scripture is equally clear about something our culture desperately needs to hear:
Jesus entered our broken world without participating in our sin.
Love does not require God to rename darkness as light.
Christ comes near enough to touch sinners while remaining holy enough to save them.
And this is where John 1:14 becomes even more beautiful.

But ἐσκήνωσεν — eskēnōsen carries the sense of dwelling or pitching one's tent. This is why commentators often render the thought as “tabernacled among us.” The wording naturally recalls the biblical tabernacle—the dwelling associated with God's presence among His people.
Long before Bethlehem, Israel knew the imagery of God's presence dwelling among His people.
God desires to dwell among His people.
Then John looks at Jesus and effectively tells us:
God's presence has come among us in a way the tent in the wilderness anticipated but could never accomplish.
That combination confronts both kinds of people hiding from God.
Some hide because they think their sin is too terrible for grace.
Others hide because they refuse to admit that their sin actually is sin.
Truth tears the mask from our faces.
Grace refuses to throw the exposed sinner away.
Grace meets the repentant sinner there.
This is why Jesus is dangerous to hypocrisy and irresistible to the brokenhearted.
You cannot stand before Christ indefinitely pretending.
Eventually the mask becomes too heavy.
And perhaps yours is heavy now.
Maybe people come to you for prayer while your own prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary so well that nobody realizes how far your heart has wandered.
But something between you and Jesus has become cold.
Here is the scandalous beauty of John 1:14:
Because love was determined to rescue sinners from it.
Jesus did not enter the world merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came for people whose histories could embarrass them.
People who had made themselves scandals.
People other people had turned into scandals.
And ultimately, people who discovered that underneath all the carefully managed appearances was the same desperate human condition:
That is why the incarnation cannot be reduced to a Christmas decoration.
The kingdom of darkness is being confronted.
God's promise is taking on flesh.
And the road from the manger leads eventually toward Golgotha.
Paul captures the descent in Philippians 2: Christ, existing in the form of God, humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
The One above us came among us.
The Holy One came for sinners.
The Author entered His own story.
And humanity did what fallen humanity does.
But even that became the stage upon which grace displayed its unimaginable depth.
Because the cross was not Jesus losing control of the story.
The cross was central to the saving mission for which He came.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose.
The grave could not write His ending.
Your sin does not have to write yours either.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance magically restores every relationship.
It does not mean Christians never suffer again.
Biblical grace is far deeper than motivational optimism.
It means the repentant sinner can be forgiven.
The condemned can be justified through faith in Christ.
The estranged can be reconciled to God.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The enslaved can begin walking in freedom.
The sinner can become a child of God—not because the sinner rewrote the record, but because Jesus Christ became flesh, went to the cross, and rose again.
This is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Jesus came for sinners like me.
Maybe you have spent your entire life around Christianity without surrendering yourself to Christ.
You know when to say amen.
But knowing Christian things is not the same as knowing Christ.
John's Gospel will later tell us why it was written: so that people may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing they may have life in His name.
And perhaps this is the moment you finally stop negotiating with Jesus.
You do not need another year of hiding.
You do not need another carefully constructed version of yourself.
The religious person who secretly knows religion has become a substitute for intimacy with Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door and calls you to follow Jesus out.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished response. Be honest.

Not because typing words saves anyone. Christ saves. But sometimes a public sentence becomes the moment somebody stops protecting the mask and begins admitting what God has already been showing the heart.
Someone reading the same comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting through a dark season.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
If Christ has given you truth, carry truth.
If grace found you, point someone else toward grace.
The brother who has stopped attending church.
The daughter quietly questioning whether God cares.
The believer who failed and assumes Christians will never let him forget it.
The person who does not believe in Jesus but might finally read something because you shared it.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience and love—not through financial transactions.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way believers participate in helping biblical truth reach more people.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith.
But because Gospel ministry requires people willing to pray, participate, share, give, encourage, and help truth travel farther than it otherwise would.
If you want to support that mission and go deeper with us:
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to their pain.
Because perhaps they have heard plenty about Christians.
Perhaps they have heard plenty about churches.
Perhaps they have heard plenty about religion.
But maybe they have never truly encountered the staggering announcement John placed before the world:
God did not save us by shouting instructions from a safe distance.
Near enough to carry a cross.
And powerful enough to rise again.
So when shame tells you God would never come near someone like you, remember Bethlehem.
When suffering tells you God cannot understand, remember the incarnation.
When sin tells you there is no road home, remember the cross.
When death tells you every story eventually belongs to the grave, remember the empty tomb.
And when your past whispers that the scandal is the final chapter, remember Jesus.
Because perhaps the most astonishing truth of “the Word became flesh” is not merely that God entered human history.
It is that in Jesus Christ, God entered a world filled with sinners to rescue them—and He is still calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Your scandal may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Your failure may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have authority to become your savior or your master.
Your worst chapter may tell the truth about what you did.
But the cross tells the greater truth about what Christ has done.
And the empty tomb tells you that Jesus still specializes in endings everyone else thought were already written.
The Word became flesh because God was not willing to leave redemption as a distant promise—He came personally to bring sinners home.
